units.title: Unit 31 — The environment
learningObjectives: Use idiomatic combinations for waste disposal, recycling, pollutants and threats to public health.
Explain climate-change consequences with precise collocations for extreme temperatures, flooding and irreversible damage.
Discuss emissions, renewable energy and mitigation strategies using natural formal and everyday language.
Avoid misleading combinations such as very vital, soaring heat and energy origins.

items.example: The disposal of household waste became a priority after the town's landfill closed.
items.note: Disposal of waste is the formal noun phrase for the process of getting rid of rubbish safely.

items.example: Several businesses were prosecuted for trying to dump waste beside the river.
items.note: Dump waste implies abandoning or depositing waste improperly rather than disposing of it responsibly.

items.example: The council collects household waste on Mondays and recyclable materials on Thursdays.
items.note: Household waste means rubbish generated in people's homes, not primarily industrial refuse.

items.example: The coating was replaced because its ingredients were harmful to the environment.
items.note: Harmful to takes the preposition to; it describes something that can damage nature or health.

items.example: The factory plans to recycle waste instead of sending every material to landfill.
items.note: Recycle waste describes processing discarded material for reuse, not merely collecting it.

items.example: The laboratory contracted a specialist to remove toxic waste from its storeroom.
items.note: Toxic waste contains poisonous substances and requires stricter handling than ordinary rubbish.

items.example: Poor drinking-water quality can create a serious risk to public health.
items.note: Public health concerns the wellbeing of a population rather than a single patient's medical care.

items.example: A major oil spill could become an environmental catastrophe for the coastal wetlands.
items.note: Environmental catastrophe describes exceptionally large-scale and destructive ecological harm.

items.example: Changes in ocean temperature can disrupt fishing communities on a global scale.
items.note: On a global scale refers to consequences or action across the world rather than in one locality.

items.example: Local students organised environmental campaigns calling for cleaner waterways.
items.note: Environmental campaigns are organised efforts to raise awareness or change behaviour on ecological issues.

items.example: Scientists are examining how climate change affects regional rainfall.
items.note: Climate change refers to long-term shifts in climate, not a short spell of unusual weather.

items.example: Water scarcity is an urgent issue for communities facing consecutive dry seasons.
items.note: Urgent issue emphasises that a problem requires prompt attention or action.

items.example: Changing weather patterns have made the start of the rainy season less predictable.
items.note: Weather patterns are recurring tendencies in weather over an area or period.

items.example: Reliable monitoring is absolutely vital during an emergency evacuation.
items.note: Absolutely is a natural intensifier with vital; very vital is not idiomatic in this sense.

items.example: If the reservoir keeps shrinking, we will have to change our ways of using water.
items.note: Change our ways means alter established habits or behaviour, usually for a better outcome.

items.example: Workers moved the outdoor inspection to dawn to avoid the searing heat.
items.note: Searing collocates with heat; it does not normally describe temperatures as searing temperatures.

items.example: When temperatures soar during a heatwave, hospitals may see more dehydration cases.
items.note: Temperatures soar means temperatures rise very sharply; soaring heat is not the usual pairing.

items.example: Rainfall stayed well above the average for the region throughout April.
items.note: Above the average compares a measurement with a stated or understood normal level.

items.example: Three days of heavy rain caused widespread flooding across the valley.
items.note: Widespread describes flooding affecting many places, not just one flooded street.

items.example: The research team checks river quality on a regular basis.
items.note: On a regular basis is a slightly formal alternative to regularly for repeated activity.

items.example: Ignoring early warnings could have dire consequences for small island communities.
items.note: Dire consequences means extremely serious negative outcomes, often used in warnings.

items.example: The report warns against processes that may lead to irreversible climate change.
items.note: Irreversible means a change cannot realistically be undone; it is stronger than long-lasting.

items.example: Taking fewer unnecessary flights can help us reduce our carbon footprint.
items.note: Reduce one's carbon footprint means cut the emissions attributable to personal or organisational activity.

items.pt: distância percorrida pelos alimentos até o consumidor
items.example: The shop publishes food miles to help customers compare delivery distances.
items.note: Food miles measures how far food travels from production to consumption, not its nutritional value.

items.example: The restaurant relies on local produce whenever nearby farms can meet demand.
items.note: Local produce typically means food grown or made nearby, especially fresh agricultural products.

items.example: The company intends to offset carbon emissions from essential business flights.
items.note: Offset emissions means compensate through reductions or removals elsewhere; it does not itself eliminate the original emissions.

items.example: The city is measuring vehicle emissions near its busiest crossroads.
items.note: Vehicle emissions are pollutants released by cars and other road vehicles, not vehicle transmissions.

items.example: Several older power stations are being replaced by cleaner sources of electricity.
items.note: Power station is the usual noun phrase for a facility that generates electricity.

items.example: Her new hybrid car uses both a conventional engine and an electric motor.
items.note: A hybrid car combines different power sources; mixed car is not the conventional term.

items.example: The island is exploring alternative energy sources to reduce its dependence on diesel.
items.note: Energy sources is the standard noun phrase; energy origins is not natural here.

items.example: The community centre installed solar heating to reduce its energy bills.
items.note: Solar heating uses energy from the sun; sun heating is not the conventional expression.

items.example: The coastal region plans to build offshore wind farms away from major shipping lanes.
items.note: Offshore wind farms are installations at sea, in contrast to onshore wind farms on land.

items.pt: as reservas de petróleo se esgotam
items.example: If oil supplies run dry, transport systems will need other sources of energy.
items.note: Run dry means become exhausted or depleted; it can describe supplies of oil or water.

items.example: The district wants renewable energy to supply most public buildings by 2035.
items.note: Renewable energy comes from sources naturally replenished on a human timescale.

items.example: Better insulation can make a real difference to household energy consumption.
items.note: Make a difference is idiomatic for producing a meaningful effect; real strengthens the impact.

items.example: The proposal would introduce green taxes on particularly polluting products.
items.note: Introduce taxes means put new taxation measures into effect; present taxes is not equivalent.

items.example: The housing cooperative chose eco-friendly design principles for its new buildings.
items.note: Eco-friendly modifies products or designs intended to have a reduced environmental impact.

items.example: Engineers are trying to find a solution to the recurring water leaks.
items.note: Find a solution is the natural combination; give a solution is usually not intended.

items.example: New energy standards are one way to combat climate change in the long term.
items.note: Combat climate change is a formal, purposeful alternative to fight climate change.

items.example: The scientists decided to sound a warning before the contamination spread.
items.note: Sound a warning means issue a public or serious caution about a likely danger.

items.example: Soaring temperatures forced the marathon organisers to shorten the route.
items.note: Soaring modifies temperatures, whereas searing normally modifies heat.

units.title: Unit 32 — Town and country life
learningObjectives: Distinguish natural descriptions of urban living, busy streets and services from those of rural isolation.
Use phrases describing housing, urban regeneration, green spaces and transport in authentic contexts.
Differentiate crowded streets from congested roads, and informal rural idioms from formal planning terminology.
Describe villages and landscapes using precise adjective-noun collocations and recognise register differences.

items.example: The bustling city centre attracts visitors well into the evening.
items.note: Bustling describes a place full of movement and activity, not necessarily overcrowded or unpleasant.

items.example: For her, urban living offers cultural events and convenient transport.
items.note: Urban living is a relatively formal equivalent of city life.

items.example: Reliable public transport makes it easier for residents to leave their cars at home.
items.note: Reliable means a transport service runs consistently as expected, unlike merely frequent transport.

items.example: The local supermarket has long opening hours to serve evening commuters.
items.note: Long opening hours refers to shops or services staying open for extended periods.

items.example: A busy lifestyle leaves some professionals little time for weekday shopping.
items.note: Busy lifestyle refers to a person's demanding pattern of daily activities.

items.example: The estate agent presented an extensive range of flats in different neighbourhoods.
items.note: Extensive range is a promotional collocation stressing a large variety of choices.

items.example: Prospective buyers toured the show houses before choosing a floor plan.
items.note: Show houses are furnished model homes used to display housing developments.

items.example: Visitors can take a virtual tour of the museum before booking tickets.
items.note: Take a virtual tour means explore a place digitally rather than visiting in person.

items.example: The farmhouse retains its rustic charm despite the modern kitchen.
items.note: Rustic charm is the appealing, simple and traditional quality of a country place.

items.example: The cabin sits in the back of beyond, though the nearest village is only twenty kilometres away.
items.note: In the back of beyond is an informal expression for a very remote place.

items.example: After years downtown, they dreamed of a rural idyll beside a quiet lake.
items.note: A rural idyll is an idealised image of peaceful countryside life, often contrasting with reality.

items.example: The old fishing town remained a quiet backwater long after the nearby port expanded.
items.note: Quiet backwater often suggests a place removed from major events or development.

items.example: We found a small café in the middle of nowhere on the mountain road.
items.note: In the middle of nowhere emphasises isolation and may be humorous or critical.

items.example: Without any activities during the delay, the children were bored rigid.
items.note: Bored rigid is informal and emphatic: extremely bored.

items.example: Crowded streets made walking through the old quarter difficult during the festival.
items.note: Crowded streets usually focuses on the presence of many people, unlike congested roads which focus on traffic.

items.example: After the move, he needed time to adjust to the hectic pace of life downtown.
items.note: Hectic pace of life stresses constant activity and pressure rather than simple busyness.

items.example: It was impossible to hail a taxi outside the theatre during the downpour.
items.note: Hail a taxi means signal to an available taxi on the street, not pre-book a ride.

items.example: The foundation opened a youth centre in the inner city.
items.note: Inner city generally refers to older central urban districts, sometimes associated with social disadvantage.

items.example: The council approved urban regeneration funding for the disused industrial district.
items.note: Urban regeneration means renewing or improving declining urban areas through coordinated investment.

items.example: Several derelict buildings will be converted into studios and affordable homes.
items.note: Derelict buildings are neglected and in poor condition, not simply old.

items.example: The neighbourhood launched a tree-planting scheme to increase shade along local streets.
items.note: A tree-planting scheme is an organised programme to add trees, often for environmental benefits.

items.example: Families seeking more green space moved to the leafy suburbs.
items.note: Leafy suburbs evokes residential districts with many trees and often a pleasant atmosphere.

items.example: Improved parks have made the district a desirable place to live.
items.note: Desirable place to live is common in housing promotion and planning contexts.

items.example: The planning application proposes thirty new residential dwellings near the station.
items.note: Residential dwellings is formal planning language for homes or housing units.

items.example: Congested roads delayed deliveries throughout the morning.
items.note: Congested roads refers to heavy vehicle traffic; crowded streets may instead refer to pedestrians.

items.example: Better lighting was introduced as part of a plan to reduce night-time crime.
items.note: Night-time crime is an urban-planning phrase for offences committed after dark.

items.pt: a uma distância que pode ser percorrida a pé
items.example: The new library is within walking distance of the railway station.
items.note: Within walking distance means close enough to reach on foot without difficulty.

items.example: Some corner shops are open all hours, even on public holidays.
items.note: Open all hours is an informal expression for very long, sometimes nearly continuous, opening times.

items.example: The housing project includes recreational facilities such as a sports court and playground.
items.note: Recreational facilities is formal wording for spaces or equipment intended for leisure activities.

items.example: The new district will include commercial facilities on the ground floors.
items.note: Commercial facilities refers to premises and services used for business activity, such as shops.

items.example: She missed city life after spending a year in a remote village.
items.note: City life is a more everyday alternative to the more formal urban living.

items.example: The new bypass should divert vehicles away from busy roads near the school.
items.note: Busy roads emphasises substantial traffic, while congested roads implies that movement is restricted.

items.example: The hiking trail crosses miles of unspoilt countryside with few modern developments.
items.note: Unspoilt describes rural land that has not been significantly damaged by development.

items.example: From the ridge, we could see rolling countryside stretching towards the coast.
items.note: Rolling countryside typically has gentle hills, rather than flat land or steep mountains.

items.example: The village market attracts farmers from the surrounding countryside.
items.note: Surrounding countryside refers to rural land around a particular place.

items.example: The photographers documented changes in the rural landscape after the new road opened.
items.note: Rural landscape is a neutral phrase describing the visible character of country areas.

items.pt: paisagem árida e desprovida de vegetação
items.example: The old quarry left a barren landscape with little vegetation.
items.note: Barren landscape describes land with little growth or fertility, often stark or empty.

items.example: The hikers admired the rugged landscape from the mountain pass.
items.note: Rugged landscape suggests rough ground, dramatic contours or steep terrain.

items.example: A picturesque village lies beside the river at the end of the valley.
items.note: Picturesque village highlights an attractive, charming appearance suitable for a photograph.

items.example: The small coastal village depends on fishing and seasonal tourism.
items.note: Coastal village is a neutral combination for a settlement beside the sea.

items.example: Medical teams travelled for hours to reach the remote village.
items.note: Remote village emphasises geographical isolation or difficulty of access.

items.example: A weekly bus now connects the town with several outlying villages.
items.note: Outlying villages are settlements further from the centre of a district or urban area.

items.example: The old fortress seems to dominate the landscape above the river.
items.note: Dominate the landscape means stand out as the most visually prominent feature.
